title: The Geometry of Self
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Buddhist teaching of non-self, anatta, one of the three marks of reality alongside dukkha and anicca. A seven-day retreat in Canada supplies the central story: Nomon sees the head organizer's name on the practice discussion sheet, panics, and then glimpses personality as a geometric shape with pokey corners that can be carried without fear. Nomon then tells of Shenxiu and Huineng and their two poems, ending on "where does the dust alight?" The evening closes with a reading from Ajahn Amaro's Small Boat, Great Mountain, where a young seeker leaves England, wanders the beaches of Thailand, and finds the cheerful monks of Ajahn Chah's forest monastery, learning that freedom was already within.

sentences.text: It's nice, the lighting like this.
It feels like we're in the living room.
If you want to get cozy, not too bright, if you want to have a little snooze, go right ahead.
Several of us were here on Saturday, and we had a really lovely all-day Zen sit, 6 in the morning until 9 at night.
It's better not to add up how many hours that is, but in conventional time it seems like a long time.

Conventional time is not necessarily your friend when you're approaching these things, because you could think to yourself, "Well, I can come on Wednesday night and I can sit for a total of an hour and a bit, but then my knee hurts a little bit.
That's like 15 hours, so my knee would fall off."
It's logical.
It's better not to think about it that way.
It actually is very beautiful.
What happens is, you sit for a while, and conventional time is not quite as convincing.
You can enter into dream time.
One of the things I love the most about sitting all day is the way the light gradually moves across the room from morning to night.
In this case it's dark, light, dark.
One has one's moments, and sometimes it seems like it's dragging on and difficult, but other times it's just so beautiful to watch the light and let the mind do what the mind needs to do.
So this evening I thought I'd take a stab at saying something about the confusing Buddhist teaching of not-self or non-self, and so I'm calling this talk The Geometry of Self.
I mentioned this at noon today and Edie immediately said, "But there is no self," which is exactly the point.
We've all heard this, I think, and it's pretty confusing that Buddhism seems to be saying there's no self, no person.
But I feel like a person.
Don't you feel like a person?
And the Buddhist teachings also seem to emphasize one's own direct experience, that you should not just try to talk yourself into some dogma or some teaching.
The teachings may guide you or encourage you or provide you with some tools or new angles on things, but really it's not real until you can see it for yourself and experience it for yourself.
So on the face of it, this seems like it's going to really work out like no self.
It really feels like there's a self.
I feel like somebody with an identity and a history and tendencies and wishes and desires and values.
Think of the vast vocabulary we've developed to describe this sort of thing that we call the self.
But it turns out the Buddhist doctrine of non-self is not denying that experience.
What it's saying is that we've come to some mistaken conclusions.
These experiences and thoughts and emotions which we pull together and impute this self from are maybe not exactly the whole story, maybe not exactly real in the way that we think they are.
And so the Buddhist teachings of non-self are saying there's a self and there's also not a self, and there's also not not a self.
The Pali term is anata, which literally means, "a" means not, the prefix, and "nata" is one of the words for self.
So it means not self.
That's a pretty literal translation.
And anata is one of a set of three really fundamental teachings, fundamental concepts in Buddhism.

The Buddha taught from the very beginning that not only do we not come to accurate conclusions about the nature of self, our conclusions about the very nature of reality and experience are a little off.
And the reason they're a little off is that we're in some ways in denial, or not really understanding in a direct way, the three fundamental aspects of reality.
They called these the three marks of reality, three marks of dharmas, and anata is one of the three, this non-self.
So now already we're hearing that this teaching of non-self doesn't just apply to what we call the self.
Somehow it has a broader connotation, something universal about reality is pointed to by this teaching of anata, of not self.
And the other two are unsatisfactoriness, or the Pali word is dukkha, which also gets translated as suffering.
No translation of that word in English is really quite satisfactory.

It has many aspects and angles, but the essential point in this context is that we tend to seek lasting satisfaction from things that are not going to last, from things that are not really going to support that desire.
And therefore we're serially disappointed, you know what I mean?
There are obvious examples from Western materialism, which we're too hip for, but we have to admit if we look at it we fall into that as well as anybody.
If you only had fill in the blank, and then you get fill in the blank, and it's not quite what I thought.
And there's a better one.
This drives the world economy too, right?
That's why they can sell the new iPods every year.
Here's a side point: a high percentage of iPod sales now are to people who already own one or more iPods.
So there's always a better one.
So dukkha is the second one.
There's more angles to it, but for now, things not quite being satisfactory or satisfying in the way that we think they should be.
They're deeply satisfying in ways beyond this, but for now, dukkha.
And then the third of the three marks is anicca, which means impermanence.
So anata, dukkha, and anicca.
I don't really think that to practice you have to learn and memorize lots of terms in five different languages.

But these three would be good to learn, because the English translations, even when they're pretty straightforward and literal, like not-self or non-self, have so many other connotations that they confuse us and we miss the boat.
So it's not the worst to learn these three terms: anata, dukkha, anicca.
One of the things I appreciate about anicca, about impermanence, is that it's so obvious, you know what I mean?
It seems like, why would you even bother to say that?
Everyone knows that everything's impermanent.
But if you think about our attitude towards impermanence, we don't really quite believe in it.
The way we tend to be, if you notice, is that things are permanent for a little while, at least.
Then they're impermanent.
So we basically include impermanence in the concept of later.
We don't really believe in impermanence right now, which is part of why death is so hard.
And by the way, another aside: I had put another name on the altar.
Alfreda Goetz is Margie Goetz's mom.
She died on Saturday.
She was in her middle 90s and had been ill.
Margie told me today that they got together at Thanksgiving and her mom was lucid and they had a nice time.
Her mom more or less said, "This is wonderful, now I can let go."
It's a very classic kind of death, the kind we like as much as we can like death.
It's just so interesting, isn't it, the way we're wanting to have things in just certain ways.
But anyway, back to Anatta.
What we've got to remember about all these things is that the Buddha was not just trying to be clever.
His central point is always freedom from suffering.
It's always liberation, always being freed up from the ways that we're caught and bound.
He was only interested in trying to analyze and understand reality to the extent that it served that purpose of freedom and liberation.
There are some lovely, well-known passages in the Pali Canon where people show up and ask him abstruse philosophical questions.
He won't answer those kinds of questions.
Like, is the nature of the universe permanent?
He wouldn't answer.
That kind of thing.

So we should always consider, when we hear a Buddhist teaching and it doesn't really make sense or it seems really philosophical or abstract, that the way to approach it is to wonder, "Well, how could this be helpful?"
One starts from the assumption: this must be helpful in some way.
Maybe I don't understand it, or maybe I'm not ready for it, or maybe it just doesn't have to be helpful to me.
I don't know, but let's start from there.
And so this teaching on non-self must have some liberating quality.
So I want to tell you a story from another sesshin.
Let me tell you a little more background on sesshin if you haven't had that experience.
To sit all day is not just about packing in a lot of meditation.
We practice quiet during the day, so there's no conversation.
The schedule and arrangements allow us to reduce our decision-making quite radically.
Well, it's still strange that the mind has all these funny little ways of finding little decisions to make even though there aren't any you have to make.
Should I stretch like this, like that?
There's always something.
But anyway, it radically reduces decision-making and creates a container in which your whole life and your whole being can settle a little bit or a lot bit.
And it can be quite peaceful and it can also be quite intense.

If the mind is strongly conditioned, as ours tend to be, to want constant trouble and stimulation and excitement, and then you tell your mind, "OK, for the next one day or three days or seven days, the big excitement is going to be a bell ringing," that can be pretty exciting, actually.
Or whether it's going to be lentil soup or miso soup or maybe that nice Mexican chili.
In this context, you can see things about the mind that you kind of know, but you don't pay a whole lot of attention to because you're busy going on to the next thing.
Busy going to work, busy going to school, busy taking care of your family, busy recreating, busy doing whatever you're doing.
And there's a tremendous sense in this practice of sesshin of the possibility for really radical insight and discovery.
There's also a kind of unmooring and disconnection from the usual things that hold us in our usual place.
So it can also be confusing and even disturbing.
But fundamentally, you're not doing much of anything.
So it's really interesting to think about how an experience of doing basically nothing could have all these different aspects, but it does.
One of the things I've often noticed in sesshin is that when we remove this steady social stimulus of reassurance, a lot can happen in the mind and in the heart.
Part of what we're doing socially all the time is reassuring each other that we're OK.
A good percentage of our social interactions have that quality, which is why it's a little bit unnerving, I think, to meet somebody new,
especially somebody that you somehow feel some attraction to, because you don't know if they're going to reassure you or not.
There's this little moment of, "Oh."
We do have a way of saying, "Hi, I'm Tim.
Would you please reassure me that I'm OK?
And if you do, I will definitely reassure you that you're OK."

So all this is taken away in sesshin, and it becomes more possible, therefore, to be aware of the actual patterns of thinking and emotion and feelings in the mind and the body, some of which are not, from that point of view, OK.
There's a tremendous amount of support in the practice of sesshin in a healthy community.
So there is a lot of support, but not that kind of mutually limiting reassurance support.
There's a sort of emptiness support, a support in which we're giving each other radically space to be whoever we actually need to be right now, not who we think we need to be right now.
In that context, sometimes you figure out that you don't know yourself quite as well as you thought you did.
And you can see ways in which that not knowing and confusion and disconnect can allow you to get way off the track of reality.
One of my favorites is that you could be sitting sesshin with somebody whom you hadn't met before, maybe sitting right next to them.
And there's a way that you really get to know them.
You know the way they walk, you know the way they sit, maybe you know the way they smell a little bit.
You know them in a way that you don't know a lot of people, this person sitting next to you at the sesshin, at the Zen retreat.
And naturally the mind then starts imputing from that a self.
So there's another way of studying not-self.
You're creating for that person itself because you don't know their story.
You don't know where they're from or what their job is or whether they like you or any of that.
And it's possible to make up a very elaborate and convincing story.
Then at the end of the retreat you seek them out to say hello and tell them that you know their story.
The first word out of their mouth, it all just crumbles in the dust, and you realize, "I made all that up."
So sesshin can help us see how convincing this story of self is.
And if we are telling that story about other people and believing it, in what ways are we doing that for ourselves?
All the time.
But it's so convincing.
When we make up a story about who we are, there's not usually another one of us inside to have that conversation and realize it was all made up.
One of the things I often notice in sesshin practice is that tendencies I have normally loom large within the quiet context of sesshin.
You know what I mean?
In our normal, socially reassured world, we're always putting our tendencies back in perspective, back in perspective, back in perspective.
"I got a little grumpy, but she was a little grumpy and that's okay."
One of my own tendencies, maybe you've noticed, is that my personality seems to become overly involved in things.
Doing a little bit too much.
Leaning into life a little more than is quite healthy for me or for others.
Not too much anymore, but a little bit.
I often do that.
Not giving people quite enough space to figure things out for themselves.
Running around organizing things a little too much.
Some people love that and some people don't like it, but it's a tendency that I have.
I'm always studying and working with it and noticing when it creates suffering.
When I create suffering in somebody else, I practice apologizing and starting over.
It's something I work with, and it doesn't usually upset me too much anymore.
But I've noticed in sesshin that I really focus on that tendency for some reason.
Partly because in a lot of the sesshin, I am one of the organizers, so there are a lot of things I need to be doing.

There are a lot of opportunities to do a little too much, or give somebody a little too much support or a little too many suggestions, or go on a little too much, or just not be quiet and give people space.
And so that's why it's really great for me to go to other sanghas' retreats.
I'm getting to a point here.
Don't worry.
Hopefully it will be helpful.
So I went to a seven-day retreat in Canada not too long ago.
I didn't really have any responsibilities there.
They had it all organized.
I didn't have to figure out who was going to do which jobs and be the smart one who knew all this stuff.
I could just go sit.
And I especially did not want to interfere with their process.
In the context of our sanghas, I know that I can cast a long shadow.
So I was really trying to be quiet.
I thought of it before the sesshin, which I don't usually do: "Okay, I'm going to work on this."
It's a little problematic in sesshin to work on things, but I did.
I wanted to work on this.
And I thought I was doing pretty well at first.
But then there are all these little impulses to help out and give somebody a little tip.
We were doing oryoki practice like we did here on Saturday, and there were several people next to me who hadn't done oryoki before.
So I tried to go a little slower and make sure my movements were obvious.
That was okay.
Then I noticed my neighbor was just not getting the thing.
Every meal I was wondering, should I say something?
He was taking his napkin and just putting it aside and not spreading it out.
I was like, I know this is not that important, and he's just having a nice sesshin.
So I didn't say anything.
But it was becoming this big theme in the mind, this big theme of "it's best to close my eyes so I wouldn't see all the mistakes."
And then there are not too many spaces in that facility to relax.
In my case, I was sewing, doing some Zen sewing.
There was only one place where you could do Zen sewing, which also happened to be the only place you could really have a meeting.
The organizers were having a meeting after lunch, and I was very careful.
I asked, "Oh, should I leave?"
And they said, "No, no, no, no, please stay, please stay.
You won't bother us."
So I'm sitting there sewing, listening to this meeting, which is the exact same meeting I've had a hundred times, trying not to say anything.
Anyway, it went on like that.
And one of the things that they did ask me to do was to give practice discussion, where people could come see me individually to discuss their practice, which is lovely.
Not that many of them knew me, so I didn't have a whole lot of business.
I just saw a few people and it was very nice.
I thought I was doing okay.
Then I was looking at the little sheet where people write down if they want to see you, and I saw on there that Kate McCandless, one of the priests, had signed up.
She's the main organizer, in this case the head organizer.
We're trying to clarify our roles, and we're using a role we haven't used before called the tanto, the head of practice.
So Kate is the head of practice, the top dog.
And she signed up to see me.

I had an intense panic attack, because I immediately came to an absolutely compelling conclusion that she had signed up to talk to me individually so she could chew me out for my endless meddling ways, my constant interference.
It was very intense.
And then I thought, "Whoa," and saw it internally.
And I thought, well, what is that?
Why am I feeling this way?
Why am I thinking that?
I wasn't quite sure if it was real or not, but I had enough space, with several days of sitting, to think, "Wow, what is that?
What's under that?"
I wondered.
And then I saw fear, really powerful fear under that.
What I realized the fear seemed to be about was the fear that I am crippled in a certain way, that I have a certain personality which is never going to allow true intimacy with others.
This particular tendency, which I was studying as if in a microscope, and when you look in a microscope, things get big, right?
It's just going to prevent that, and it's a really strong fear.
And then I had this kind of realization, which is getting to not-self: that my personality, our personality, is a kind of geometric shape, almost, which has formed over many years.

A little bit because of our choices or our input, but largely through many other factors: the way we were brought up, our society, our culture, previous lives maybe, if you go in for that kind of thing.
Our personality is like this geometrical shape that's been created in all these different ways, and it's something we carry around, because that's what human beings do.
That's how we function in the world.
It would be impossible, and probably really unhealthy, to try to get rid of this shape.
But this shape has little pokey places that stick out, and sometimes your pokey places might bump into somebody else's pokey places, but that's not you either.
That's just a sharp corner.
I'm picturing these little tendrils or something coming out of this thing.
The visualization is just shifting.
And I had a really powerful feeling, in an instant, of "I don't have to be afraid for my shape."
My shape is my responsibility.
Nobody else has this particular shape.
I need to work with it to reduce trouble, but I can really let go of that strong identification with personality.
Of course, a few minutes later it all comes rushing back, but I think that's a little bit of what the Buddha was trying to talk about.
Through practice, you may come to see this complex of thinking and emotion and personality and whatever else.
We have many different tools and ways of looking at this, the vast literature of pop psychology and real psychology and all of this, all of which are just concepts, right?
None of them are exactly it, and so your personality may never look like a geometric shape to you.
It really did for me.
I could see it for a second.
It was kind of a prism, kind of.

But in the quiet of meditation, with the mind prepared a little bit, aware of the possibility that these thoughts, this personality, these tendencies are not me, in that solid, stuck way that I sometimes think they are, there's a little space and a little bit of liberation.
The other thing about it is that it's a vicious cycle, too, right?
One has certain tendencies, one gets worried about having certain tendencies, one gets afraid about having certain tendencies, and the tendencies get more intense.
You know what I mean?
I could really see the way I was doing that.
Of course, by the way, when Kate came to see me, it was nothing to do with me.
She wanted to talk about her own problems.
Her own shape has given her trouble.
So it's a little bit like the story of the sixth ancestor, to bring it back to Zen.
Do you know the story of the sixth ancestor?
Supposedly, in China, long ago, there was a Zen monastery with an important teacher, one of the most famous teachers in northern China, and a pretty big community.
There was a head monk in the community who was the obvious successor.
Along comes this other fellow.
The head monk, I always forget his name.
I think I put it down here.
Oh, here it is.
I forgot to write down the teacher's name, which I've forgotten too, but the head monk's name was Shenxiu.
Shenxiu was a very smart guy, very hardworking, very upright and outstanding, and probably immaculate.
Probably his robes were carefully tended and he did everything right.
We all know somebody like this, right?
Head of the class.
And this other guy came along named Huineng.
Huineng was not that way.
He was a rough sort of character, grew up in poverty, got interested in practice kind of by accident, and was illiterate.
He didn't have school where he was growing up.
When he showed up, they sent him to work in the kitchen, as you would do, right?
And one time the teacher of the monastery said, supposedly, that he was ready to decide if he would have a successor.
This is all predicated on the wonderful Zen myth of a linear, ancestral lineage: one teacher, one student, and it goes along like that.
So he announced a poetry contest to clarify who really understood Zen, and who would be his worthy successor.
And of course everybody assumed that the head monk, Shenxiu, would be the one.
And of course Shenxiu, humbly waiting a little while, was the first one to write his poem on the wall or something.
And here's his poem.
So this is how we usually think about ourselves.
This is his understanding of Dharma, and it's true as far as it goes.
*The body is a Bodhi tree.
The mind is a standing mirror, bright.
At all times, polish it diligently, and let no dust alight.*
*The body is a Bodhi tree.
The mind is a standing mirror, bright.
At all times, polish it diligently, and let no dust alight.*
So take care of everything very carefully.
Go to therapy.
Clean up your problems.
Clean up your house.
Do everything just so.
Take care of this self.
Polish it up.
You want your shape to be a beautiful, smooth, shiny egg or something like that.
So that was his understanding, and that's kind of what we all think, right?
If I just try hard enough.
If I just polish the mirror.
If I could just improve.
We might be a little discouraged.
We might not have as much confidence as Shenxiu.
We might not really think we can do this, but we think that that's how it goes.
And so the rough character, Huineng, hearing this, knew in a flash that was not how it is.
He could just somehow see the other side of that.
See the emptiness of that.
And he had to have one of his buddies in the kitchen write this out for him on the wall, because he couldn't write.
His response was:
*Bodhi is no tree, nor is the mind a standing mirror bright.
Since all is originally empty, where does the dust alight?*
Where does the dust alight?
Yeah.
*Bodhi is no tree, nor is the mind a standing mirror bright.
Since all is originally empty, where does the dust alight?*
So are our problems really problems?
Where are your problems?
In here?
What are they sticking to?
Can the dust really land anywhere?
And so, of course, we need both poems, which is the point of the story.
Sometimes the story is misunderstood to be like, the first guy was a big loser, and he didn't get it.
He tried too hard, and too bad for him.
And the second guy was like, but you need both.
It's both two halves of one coin.
We need to take care of this self and realize there's no self here.
There's no self to take care of.
It's all just fill in the blank.
No words are right.
I hope this was in some way helpful.

I wanted to share with you a little bit about my experience of anatta and hope that it will encourage you to study this, and not just with your thinking, but with your heart, with your body, with your senses.
But also to consider in our thinking: how do we think about ourselves?
Is that way of thinking about ourselves accurate?
And more importantly, does that way of thinking about ourselves bring us joy, or does it create suffering?
In Western culture, we're quite concerned about what's right and what's wrong.
I think it might be more helpful for us to de-emphasize that particular duality in our life, and maybe we can help our culture that way.
Is it really that helpful to worry about what's right?
What did it feel like the last time you tried hard to be right, or the last time you were really upset about being wrong?
Are those helpful concepts?
And so we're so lucky that we have this practice handed down to us, that we can create a container, a space, some tools that we never would have thought of on our own.
Who would have thought of doing Zen?
Well, that was my first topic, and I want to read to you a little bedtime story.
Please don't take my story too literally.
Please don't be doing meditation to try to see your shape, because it won't be that for you.
You know what I mean?
Or it wasn't that for you.
The other thing about these kinds of realizations is not to think that you aren't having a realization all the time.
We're always realizing the nature of reality.
It's just we usually don't notice.
So please also don't misunderstand us and think that I'm like a super-meditator and I figured something out that you couldn't have figured out.
You already figured this out.
But maybe you didn't notice, or maybe you forgot.
And I've luckily had to give a talk, so it forced me to think about it.
Remember.
I want to read you a little bit from Ajahn Amaro, a book I've really been appreciating.
He's English, born in England, and he's a Theravadan monk in the Thai forest tradition.
So the guys that have the sort of orangey robes with one shoulder bare and follow the longer list of rules for monks.
And he studied in...
Well, I'll give it away.
Here's what he said about his early studies, and it touches a little bit on what I was saying.
I was just so appreciating his story and the way he explains the teachings.
Time to do this with you.
Yes, we do.
Everybody doing okay?
The other thing that's neat about this particular book, which is called...
I don't know why it's called this, but it's called *Small Boat, Great Mountain*, is that it's talks from a retreat with a Tibetan Dzogchen teacher.
So seemingly different ends of the Buddhist spectrum.

They were interested to look at commonalities, and so I think it gives his teachings an extra clarity, because he's not trying to figure out how his stuff's like Tibet or not like Tibet, but I think the way he was teaching was all the more clear in that context.
So first he introduces himself.
*Probably like many people, I wrestled at length with the question of freedom in the 19th and early 20s.
I was a late flower child, having been born in 1956.
I just caught the tail end of the good stuff.
And through most of my early years, I worshipped the idea of freedom and longed for the true experience of it.
Rather than becoming a bomb-throwing anarchist, though, I became more of a flower-waving, philosophical anarchist.*
*Nevertheless, I took this aspiration to freedom very seriously, and I had a profound intuition that freedom is possible.
And there is this potential we have as human beings to be totally free and that there's something utterly pure, uninhibited, and uninhibitable within us.*
Uninhibitable.
*My experience, however, was one of colliding with endless restrictions and frustrations.
First it was getting away from my parents.
Then it was the law.
Then it was not having enough money.
I thought that this or that was standing in the way of freedom.
And if only it wasn't there, I would then be free, and I was completely bewildered.
No matter how much I tried to be free and unhindered by conventions, forms and structures, mostly by defying these things, there always seemed to be another layer and another layer and another layer.
I kept meeting up with limitations.
And as a result, I was constantly feeling frustrated.
I really had no idea why.*
*I left England and began my travels in hopes of finding freedom somewhere, anywhere.
I went to Southeast Asia and pursued a Dionysian lifestyle of eat, drink, be merry, sex, drugs, rock and roll, dancing in the moonlight on the beaches*
Or certain beaches in Thailand in the seventies, where that's all that was happening, with one hand waving free.
But inside, waving free, what was the other hand doing?
It doesn't say.
*But inside me was a feeling that I was coming to a desperate crunch, to the end of the line.
I knew intuitively that this decadent path really was not leading to freedom.
So I searched some more.
I took off to the northeast of Thailand, where hardly any western tourists ever went.
I found myself wandering into a forest monastery.
It was a branch of Ajahn Chah's monastery, where his western monks lived.
It's important to know that the Thai forest tradition is the stiff end of an already narrow orthodoxy.
It's a very strict observance of an already conservative tradition.
And this was immediately apparent to me.
But what was immediately apparent to me, however, was that these people were living the most bizarrely austere life, yet they also were very cheerful.
They were the most cheerful characters I've ever met.
And here they were, getting up at three o'clock in the morning, eating one meal a day, drinking a cup of tea twice a week, sleeping on thin grass mats, having no sex,*
Definitely no sex.
*no drugs, no alcohol, and no rock and roll.
And yet they were fully at ease, very friendly, and uncomplicated people.
And I asked myself, what have they got to laugh about?
How come they're so happy when their lifestyle is so restricted?
And then I met Ajahn Chah, the teacher.
If I thought the monks seemed pretty content with their lot, meeting him was even more striking.
Ajahn Chah appeared to be the happiest man in the world.
He'd been living as a monk in the forest without any sex, music, or drink for forty years.
You would imagine someone would be pretty dried up by then.
But here was a man who was totally at ease with life.
In fact, he was thoroughly enjoying it, totally content.*
The monastery routine, monastery, oops, very much, it's only a little bit, they did warn us not to put water on the floor.
*Now the monastery routine was extremely restrained.*
Oh, got something going here.
*It aimed at simplifying all the externals, so one could put one's attention directly and pointedly on the one place where one can find freedom, in the inner world.
So rather than monastery life being a negation of the sense world, or criticism, hatred, or fear of it, the whole lifestyle was built around simplicity of living.
It was the monk's job to pay attention, to place the attention on the inner dimension, where one could be totally free.*
